newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Nurse's brother seeks say in Saudi murder case.
newsitem.headline: Nurse's brother seeks say in Saudi murder case.

text.p: The brother of an Australian nurse murdered in Saudi Arabia is seeking power to speak on his sick mother's behalf, in a move which may allow him to demand the death penalty for two British nurses accused of the killing.

Lawyer John Keen told Reuters Frank Gilford, whose sister Yvonne was murdered last December, would apply in his home state of South Australia to be appointed guardian for his 84-year-old mother Muriel, who suffers from Alzheimer's disease.

Asked if that would give him the right to demand the death penalty if the two nurses are found guilty in Saudi Arabia, Keen said: "That should be the case, yes, if he chooses to do that in exercising his discretion as the guardian."
A verdict is expected from Saudi Arabia within days.

Michael Burnett, acting for the two British nurses, Deborah Parry, 38, and Lucille McLauchlan, 31, told Reuters the nurses would contest the application to the state's Guardianship Board and call for an independent guardian to be appointed.
The body of Yvonne Gilford, 55, was discovered in her room at the King Fahd medical complex in the Saudi city of Dhahran in December. She had been stabbed, bludgeoned and suffocated.
Under Saudi law, the victim's immediate family -- Muriel and Frank -- may demand an execution if the defendants are found guilty and the court rules the penalty is appropriate.
However, the British nurses' lawyers say the family's call must be unanimous and cannot be considered so if Muriel Gilford, is found mentally incompetent.
They have already launched action in Australia to stop Gilford from calling for the death penalty on his mother's behalf until her mental competence has been determined.

In the South Australian Supreme Court on Tuesday, Justice Len King adjourned until August 26 an application from the nurses to appoint an independent guardian -- the government-appointed public advocate -- to act on Muriel's behalf in the case.

Dick Whitington, for the nurses, told the court Frank Gilford's Adelaide lawyers on Monday had advised his Saudi lawyers that there was "considerable doubt" as to his authority to represent his mother in Saudi Arabia.
